blocks.text: One thing about the eagle remains in Job: Where the slain are, there is she. The slain, that is, the bodies of the slain or of the killed. Accordingly, the words of Christ in Matth. XXIV, 28. and Luc. XVII, 37. plainly allude to this passage: Wheresoever the carcass is, there the eagles are gathered together. The Arabs assert the same. Damir, above, on the eagle: It sees a carcass from four hundred parasangs. Again: واذا وقع علي جيفة وعليها عقبان تاخرت ولم تاكل ما دام تاكل منها [wa-idhā waqaʿa ʿalī jīfa wa-ʿalayhā ʿiqbān taʾakhkharat wa-lam taʾkul mā dām taʾkul minhā] And when it comes upon a carcass on which there are ossifrages, it withdraws and does not eat their leavings. Again: اذا وقع علي جيفة وامتلا منها [II, 758] لم يستطع الطيران حتي يثب وثبات يرفع بها نفسها طبقة بعد طبقة في الهوا [idhā waqaʿa ʿalī jīfa wa-imtalā minhā lam yastaṭiʿ al-ṭayarān ḥattā yathib wathabāt yarfaʿ bihā nafsahā ṭabaqa baʿd ṭabaqa fī al-hawā] And when it comes upon a carcass and has filled itself with it, it cannot fly until, advancing by leaps, it has raised itself into the air by degrees. But this properly belongs to the percnopterus, or gypaeetus, a degenerate kind of eagle of vulturine appearance, which alone of the eagles carries off dead bodies, as Pliny ^{c)} has it from Aristotle ^{b)}. That the percnos, which is also the morphnos, differs greatly from the percnopterus is clear from the same Pliny. For in him the percnos, or morphnos, is the eagle of the third kind, and the percnopterus of the fourth. And the descriptions of the two differ considerably from each other. But Suidas, not knowing this, attributed to the percnos, or morphnos (which is the same), what is proper to the percnopterus. His words are: Μόρφνος· εἶδος ἀετοῦ· μόνοι δὲ οὗτοι τῶν ἀετῶν οὐ κυνηγητοῦσιν, ἀλλὰ νεκροῖς σώμασι τρέφονται· [Morphnos; eidos aetou; monoi de houtoi tōn aetōn ou kynēgētousin, alla nekrois sōmasi trephontai] Morphnos, a species of eagle; of the eagles these alone do not hunt, but feed on carcasses. [col. 176] By a like error Theophylact took the eagles of which Christ speaks for vultures. Ὥσπερ, he says, ἐπὶ νεκρὸν σῶμα συνάγονται ὀξέως οἱ ἀετοὶ, οἱ γῦπες δηλαδή· [Hōsper epi nekron sōma synagontai oxeōs hoi aetoi, hoi gypes dēladē] As the eagles, that is, the vultures, gather at once to a carcass. And Tzetzes, Chil. 5, ch. 9, denies that the eagle kind touches carcasses in any way; his words are:
Λέοντες θῆρες, σὺν αὐτοῖς καὶ ἀετῶν τὸ γένος, Νεκρῶν οὐκ ἀπογεύονται τὸ σύνολον σωμάτων· [Leontes thēres, syn autois kai aetōn to genos, Nekrōn ouk apogeuontai to synolon sōmatōn]

Lions, the beasts, and with them the eagle kind, do not taste dead bodies at all. Unless exceptions are added to so general a statement, its truth will not stand, as what has already been adduced amply proves. These are further confirmed by the words of Solomon, Proverb. XXX, 17: The eye that mocks his father and despises the instruction of his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it. For rebellion against parents was then a capital crime, as is clear from Exod. XXI, 15. 17. Levit. XX, 9. and Deuter. XXI, 18. And the bodies of the condemned remained unburied, exposed to wild beasts and carnivorous birds. Nor is it without reason that Solomon mentions the eye, since in the whole body no part is so exposed to the attacks of birds of prey. Hence Epictetus, explaining the sense of the old adage Κρεῖττον εἶναι ἐς κόρακας ἀπελθεῖν, ἢ ἐς κόλακας· [Kreitton einai es korakas apelthein, ē es kolakas] It is better to go to the ravens than to flatterers, says: Οἱ μὲν κόρακες τῶν τελευτηκότων τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς λυμαίνονται, ὅταν αὐτῶν οὐδέν ἐστι χρεία· οἱ δὲ κόλακες τῶν ζώντων τὰς ψυχὰς διαφθείρουσι, καὶ τὰ τούτων ὄμματα τυφλώττουσι· [Hoi men korakes tōn teleutēkotōn tous ophthalmous lymainontai, hotan autōn ouden esti chreia; hoi de kolakes tōn zōntōn tas psychas diaphtheirousi, kai ta toutōn ommata typhlōttousi] Ravens ravage the eyes of the dead only when they are of no further use; but flatterers corrupt the souls of the living and blind their eyes ^{(4)}.
